title: Cell Structure & Microscopy
description: The basic unit of life — cell theory, organelles, plant vs animal cells, microscopy, specialised cells, and how substances move across membranes.

notes.heading: The Cell Theory
notes.body: Three principles form the foundation of biology: (1) All living things are made of one or more cells. (2) The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life — all life processes happen inside cells. (3) All cells arise from pre-existing cells through cell division. There are two main types of cells: eukaryotic cells have a membrane-bound nucleus (animals, plants, fungi, protists); prokaryotic cells (bacteria) have no nucleus — their DNA floats freely in the cytoplasm. Common misconception: viruses are NOT cells and do not fit the cell theory, as they cannot reproduce on their own.

illustration.alt: Diagram comparing a prokaryotic cell and a eukaryotic cell, with the three principles of cell theory summarised below.
illustration.caption: All living things are made of cells; eukaryotic cells have a membrane-bound nucleus, while prokaryotic cells do not.

notes.heading: Animal Cell Organelles
notes.body: Every animal cell contains: (1) Nucleus — control centre containing DNA, surrounded by a nuclear membrane. (2) Cell membrane — a selectively permeable barrier controlling what enters and exits the cell. (3) Cytoplasm — jelly-like fluid where most chemical reactions occur, containing dissolved enzymes and nutrients. (4) Mitochondria (singular: mitochondrion) — site of aerobic respiration, producing ATP (energy). Often called the 'powerhouse' of the cell. Cells with high energy demands (muscle cells, sperm cells) have many mitochondria. (5) Ribosomes — tiny structures that synthesise proteins by reading mRNA instructions. Found floating in cytoplasm or attached to rough endoplasmic reticulum.

illustration.alt: Labelled diagram of an animal cell showing the nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, cytoplasm, and cell membrane.
illustration.caption: Animal cells contain a nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, cytoplasm, and a cell membrane.

notes.heading: Plant Cell Extras
notes.body: Plant cells have all the organelles of animal cells plus three key extras: (1) Cell wall — a rigid outer layer made of cellulose. Provides structural support, prevents bursting when water enters. Makes plant cells appear more box-like and regular. (2) Large central vacuole — a membrane-bound sac filled with cell sap (water, sugars, salts). Maintains turgor pressure to keep the plant upright. When vacuoles are empty, plants wilt. (3) Chloroplasts — green organelles containing chlorophyll, the pigment that absorbs light energy for photosynthesis. Found mainly in leaf cells (palisade cells) and green stem cells, but not in root cells.

illustration.alt: Labelled comparison of an animal cell and a plant cell showing organelles and plant-only structures.
illustration.caption: Plant cells have a cell wall, chloroplasts, and a large central vacuole that animal cells lack.

notes.heading: Microscopy: Light vs Electron Microscopes
notes.body: Light microscopes use visible light and glass lenses to magnify specimens up to about ×1500. They can view living cells and are what you use in a school lab. Stain (like iodine or methylene blue) is often used to make structures visible. Electron microscopes use beams of electrons and can magnify up to ×2,000,000. They reveal ultrastructure — organelles like ribosomes and internal membranes. However, specimens must be dead and in a vacuum. The formula for magnification is: magnification = size of image ÷ size of real object. Always use the same units! Example: an image of a cell measures 50 mm and the real cell is 0.05 mm. Magnification = 50 ÷ 0.05 = ×1000.

illustration.alt: Comparison of a light microscope and an electron microscope, including magnification limits and the magnification formula.
illustration.caption: Light microscopes view living cells at up to ×1500; electron microscopes reveal ultrastructure at up to ×2 000 000.

notes.heading: Specialised Animal Cells
notes.body: In multicellular organisms, cells differentiate (specialise) to perform specific functions. Key examples: (1) Red blood cells — no nucleus to maximise space for haemoglobin, biconcave disc shape for large surface area to absorb oxygen. (2) Sperm cells — streamlined head with acrosome (containing enzymes to penetrate egg), many mitochondria in the midpiece for energy, and a long tail (flagellum) for swimming. (3) Nerve cells (neurons) — long axon to carry electrical impulses over distances, branched dendrites to connect with many other neurons, myelin sheath for insulation. (4) Ciliated epithelial cells — have tiny hair-like cilia that sweep mucus and trapped particles away, found lining airways and oviducts.

illustration.alt: Diagrams of specialised cells: red blood cell, sperm cell, root hair cell, and palisade cell.
illustration.caption: Specialised cells have structural adaptations that match their function.

notes.heading: Specialised Plant Cells
notes.body: Plants also have highly specialised cells: (1) Root hair cell — long finger-like projection that massively increases surface area for absorbing water and mineral ions from soil. Has no chloroplasts (roots are underground). Has many mitochondria to power active transport of minerals. (2) Palisade cell — found in the upper layer of leaves, packed with chloroplasts for maximum light absorption. Regular column shape allows close packing. (3) Xylem vessel — dead, hollow tubes with lignin-strengthened walls that transport water and dissolved minerals upwards from roots. No cytoplasm or nucleus at maturity. (4) Guard cells — pair of kidney-shaped cells surrounding each stoma (pore). They swell or shrink to open/close stomata, controlling gas exchange and water loss.

illustration.alt: Diagrams of four specialised plant cells: root hair cell, palisade cell, xylem vessel, and guard cells.
illustration.caption: Root hair, palisade, xylem, and guard cells each have structures adapted to their function.

notes.heading: Movement Across Membranes: Diffusion and Osmosis
notes.body: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of high concentration to low concentration (down a concentration gradient) until equilibrium is reached. It is a passive process — no energy required. Examples: oxygen diffusing from alveoli into blood, CO₂ diffusing into leaves through stomata. Factors affecting diffusion rate: temperature (faster when warmer — particles have more kinetic energy), concentration gradient (steeper gradient = faster), and surface area (larger surface area = faster — why alveoli and villi are adapted this way). Osmosis is a special case of diffusion: the movement of water molecules through a selectively permeable membrane from a dilute solution (high water potential) to a concentrated solution (low water potential). In animal cells — too much water causes bursting (lysis); too little causes shrivelling (crenation). In plant cells — too much water makes them turgid (healthy); too little causes plasmolysis (wilting).

illustration.alt: Diagrams comparing diffusion of particles and osmosis of water through a membrane.
illustration.caption: Both diffusion and osmosis are passive, moving down a concentration gradient.

flashcards.definition: Control centre of the cell; contains genetic material (DNA) and controls all cell activities.
flashcards.example: Human cells each have a nucleus, except mature red blood cells.

flashcards.definition: Organelle where aerobic respiration occurs, producing ATP energy for the cell.
flashcards.example: Muscle cells have thousands of mitochondria because they need lots of energy.

flashcards.definition: A selectively permeable barrier surrounding all cells, controlling which substances enter and exit.
flashcards.example: Oxygen and glucose enter cells through the membrane; waste CO₂ leaves.

flashcards.definition: Organelle found only in plant cells and algae; contains chlorophyll and is the site of photosynthesis.
flashcards.example: Palisade cells in leaves are packed with chloroplasts.

flashcards.definition: Rigid outer layer of plant cells made of cellulose; provides structural support and prevents bursting.
flashcards.example: The box-like shape of plant cells in a microscope comes from the cell wall.

flashcards.definition: Tiny organelle that synthesises proteins by linking amino acids together following mRNA instructions.
flashcards.example: Cells producing digestive enzymes (like pancreatic cells) have many ribosomes.

flashcards.definition: Jelly-like fluid filling the cell where chemical reactions occur; contains dissolved enzymes and nutrients.
flashcards.example: Glycolysis (the first stage of respiration) takes place in the cytoplasm.

flashcards.definition: Membrane-bound sac in plant cells containing cell sap; maintains turgor pressure to support the plant.
flashcards.example: When a plant wilts, its vacuoles have lost water and the cells become flaccid.

flashcards.definition: A cell whose structure is adapted to carry out a specific function in a multicellular organism.
flashcards.example: Sperm cells have a tail for swimming; root hair cells have a long projection for absorption.

flashcards.definition: Net movement of particles from high concentration to low concentration; passive process requiring no energy.
flashcards.example: Oxygen diffuses from the lungs into the blood where oxygen concentration is lower.

flashcards.definition: Diffusion of water through a selectively permeable membrane from a dilute to a concentrated solution.
flashcards.example: Plant roots absorb water from soil by osmosis because soil water is more dilute than cell contents.

flashcards.definition: A simple cell without a membrane-bound nucleus; DNA floats free in the cytoplasm. Bacteria are prokaryotic.
flashcards.example: E. coli bacteria are prokaryotic; their DNA is a single circular chromosome.

questions.stem: Which organelle produces energy through aerobic respiration?
questions.explanation: Mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration to produce ATP, the energy currency of the cell.

questions.stem: Which structure is found in plant cells but NOT in animal cells?
questions.explanation: Plant cells have a rigid cellulose cell wall outside the cell membrane for structural support. Animal cells only have a cell membrane.

questions.stem: Where do new cells come from according to cell theory?
choices: DNA assembling itself in the cytoplasm
questions.explanation: A core principle of cell theory: all cells arise from pre-existing cells through cell division.

questions.stem: What is the function of the cell membrane?
choices: Control what substances enter and exit the cell
questions.explanation: The cell membrane is selectively permeable — it controls the movement of substances into and out of the cell.

questions.stem: What is a key difference between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells?
choices: Prokaryotes are always larger than eukaryotes
Eukaryotes always have a cell wall
questions.explanation: Prokaryotic cells (bacteria) have no membrane-bound nucleus — their DNA floats freely in the cytoplasm.

questions.stem: A student views a cell under a microscope. The image is 40 mm wide and the actual cell is 0.04 mm. What is the magnification?
questions.explanation: Magnification = image size ÷ actual size = 40 ÷ 0.04 = ×1000. Make sure units match before dividing.

questions.stem: Which of these is an adaptation of a sperm cell for its function?
choices: Biconcave disc shape to absorb oxygen
A tail (flagellum) for swimming towards the egg
questions.explanation: The sperm cell has a long tail (flagellum) and many mitochondria in the midpiece to provide energy for swimming towards the egg.

questions.stem: Why do root hair cells have no chloroplasts?
choices: Roots are underground and receive no light for photosynthesis
Root hair cells are too small to fit chloroplasts
Root hair cells use mitochondria for photosynthesis instead
questions.explanation: Roots grow underground where there is no light, so there is no need for chloroplasts. Root hair cells have many mitochondria instead to power active transport of minerals.

questions.stem: Perfume molecules spread from one corner of a room until you can smell them everywhere. Which process does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from high to low concentration. Perfume molecules spread out through the air by diffusion.

questions.stem: What would happen to an animal cell placed in pure (distilled) water?
choices: It would swell and possibly burst
Nothing — water cannot cross the membrane
It would become turgid like a plant cell
questions.explanation: Water moves into the cell by osmosis (from the dilute outside to the more concentrated cytoplasm). Without a cell wall, the animal cell may burst (lyse).

questions.stem: Which organelle synthesises (makes) proteins in a cell?
questions.explanation: Ribosomes are the sites of protein synthesis, reading mRNA instructions and linking amino acids together.

questions.stem: Why is the palisade cell well-suited for photosynthesis?
choices: It has a large surface area for absorbing water
It is packed with chloroplasts and located near the top of the leaf to catch maximum light
It has a long tail for movement
It has no nucleus to make space for chlorophyll
questions.explanation: Palisade cells are tightly packed in the upper leaf layer and contain many chloroplasts, maximising light absorption for photosynthesis.

questions.stem: A scientist wants to see the detailed internal structure of a mitochondrion. Which type of microscope should they use?
questions.explanation: Electron microscopes have much higher resolution and magnification (up to ×2,000,000), allowing scientists to see ultrastructure like the cristae inside mitochondria.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a unicellular organism?
questions.explanation: An amoeba is a single-celled (unicellular) organism. All its life processes — feeding, respiration, reproduction — happen within one cell.

questions.stem: A plant cell is placed in a concentrated salt solution. What will happen?
choices: The cell will swell and become turgid
The cell membrane will pull away from the cell wall (plasmolysis)
Nothing — plant cells are unaffected by osmosis
questions.explanation: Water leaves the cell by osmosis (moving towards the concentrated salt solution outside). The vacuole shrinks and the cell membrane pulls away from the cell wall — this is called plasmolysis.
